logline: Two incompatible flatmates navigate careers, relationships and their own worst impulses in suburban Croydon, all filmed through the lens of their most embarrassing thoughts.

renewal.note: Nine-season run concluded in December 2015. Consistently cited as one of the greatest British sitcoms ever made; no revival announced.

bollymeter.basis: A 100% Rotten Tomatoes season score established the show's formula as a genuine formal innovation in British comedy, with David Mitchell and Robert Webb delivering the defining double-act of their generation.

seasons.review_body: Peep Show launched on Channel 4 in September 2003 with a formal conceit that still feels radical: every scene shot from first-person POV, inner monologue running constantly, exposing thoughts that sitcom protagonists are supposed to keep private. The first season established Mark Corrigan and Jeremy Usbourne as one of British comedy's great duos, the timid, self-loathing loan manager and his cheerfully deluded flatmate. The season's Rotten Tomatoes score reflected the consensus that the POV technique was not a gimmick but a structural engine that made even the smallest social failure feel viscerally humiliating in the funniest possible way.

episode_reviews.title: Warring Factions
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere drops viewers into Mark's head at a house party he is constitutionally unfit for, establishing the POV format and the internal voice that makes the show work. Jeremy's breezy misanthropy is the perfect counterweight.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Mark's running internal commentary on his own disastrous small talk - the show's entire thesis delivered in a single scene.

bollymeter.basis: Widely considered an elevation on the debut, with Mark's doomed romantic pursuit of Sophie and Jeremy's escalating schemes landing some of the series' most celebrated set pieces.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 deepened the comedic engine by giving both characters more elaborate arcs. Mark's pursuit of Sophie at Jobseekers introduced a romantic through-line that would run for years, while Jeremy's scheme-of-the-week format expanded. Critics who had discovered the show in its first season cemented their enthusiasm. The series' signature mode - characters trapped by their own cowardice, making things catastrophically worse by trying to make them better - was now fully operational. The audience cult began solidifying around these episodes, which represented the first clear evidence that Peep Show was building toward something more sustained than a one-concept novelty.
seasons.season_over_season: Character arcs expand significantly in Season 2; Mark's romantic humiliations and Jeremy's musical delusions give the writers richer long-form material to run with.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 is frequently cited by critics and fans as the show's peak run, containing some of its most audacious set pieces and sharpest character writing across the full nine-season arc.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 is the episode run most frequently used to make the case for Peep Show as one of the greatest British sitcoms ever written. The Mark-Sophie relationship reaches a crisis point, Jeremy's self-sabotage becomes structurally inseparable from the comedy, and the writing by Jesse Armstrong and Sam Bain achieves a pitch-black confidence that distinguishes the show from its Channel 4 contemporaries. The Guardian later ranks the series ninth on its list of the 100 best TV shows of the 21st century, and it is these middle seasons that anchor that reputation.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 is the critical apex - blacker, tighter and more structurally confident than the debut, with Mitchell and Webb at the height of their chemistry.

bollymeter.basis: Rated 9.0 on IMDb, Season 4 is the highest-scored individual season on the platform; the wedding finale is one of the most-discussed single episodes in British comedy history.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 is the one Peep Show episode list that occasions immediate recognition among fans: it contains the series' most celebrated finale, a wedding sequence that remains a benchmark of cringe comedy executed at the level of genuine tragedy. The IMDb season rating of 9.0 is the highest individual season score in the show's run. Critics writing retrospectives on the series consistently anchor their analysis in this season's structural boldness - the way the format is weaponised not just for embarrassment but for something closer to existential despair, landing as both unbearable and hilarious simultaneously.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 takes the cringe engine to a formal peak - the wedding finale is the episode most cited when arguing the show belongs alongside Fawlty Towers and The Office in the British canon.

episode_reviews.title: Wedding
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale places Mark in a situation so perfectly constructed from his own inadequacies that escape feels both impossible and entirely his fault. The wedding sequence is the show at its formal best: hilarious, mortifying, and genuinely bleak.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The ceremony itself - a masterclass in two people failing to stop something neither truly wants.

bollymeter.basis: An 89% Rotten Tomatoes score marked the first mild critical dip, though audience appreciation remained strong; the season continued the post-wedding fallout with diminishing but solid returns.

seasons.review_body: Season 5 picked up the aftermath of the season 4 wedding, navigating the consequences with the same grim relentlessness the show had established. The slight RT dip to 89% reflected a sense among some critics that the emotional stakes had been somewhat spent in the previous season's crescendo. The writing remained sharp and the format as formally distinctive as ever, but for the first time the show was working from a position of sequel rather than escalation. Fan appreciation remained high and IMDb audience scores held. The season functioned well as a continuation if not a creative equal to its predecessor.
seasons.season_over_season: A modest step down from the Season 4 peak, working through established consequences rather than building new structural dread; still well above the standard for British comedy.

bollymeter.basis: Season 6 returned to a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score, with critics citing a creative resurgence and the introduction of new supporting dynamics that reinvigorated both leads.

seasons.review_body: Season 6 arrives as Peep Show's creative second wind. New character dynamics and a perceptible loosening of the narrative opened space for the show to find fresh modes of discomfort. The return to a perfect Rotten Tomatoes score signals renewed critical re-engagement after the slight season 5 plateau. Jesse Armstrong's writing particularly benefits from the new cast additions, and the season's standout episodes match the strongest stretches of the show's middle run. For first-time watchers coming via streaming, seasons 3, 4 and 6 provide the clearest case for the show's canonical status.
seasons.season_over_season: A genuine creative resurgence after Season 5's relative plateau; new dynamics and tighter writing brought the 100% RT score back and reminded critics why the show mattered.

bollymeter.basis: A 100% Rotten Tomatoes score sustained the show's critical standing deep into its run, a rare achievement for any sitcom in its seventh year.

seasons.review_body: Season 7 maintained its 100% Rotten Tomatoes score, which is a remarkable figure for a sitcom seven seasons into its run. The writing team continued threading long-running character consequences through largely self-contained episodes, and the show's formal skeleton was by now so well established that individual episodes could take larger risks with character behaviour. Audience response was steady, and the season contributed to the show's growing reputation as a once-in-a-generation British comedy - a show that improved on being revisited rather than running out of invention.
seasons.season_over_season: Sustains quality deep into the run; the 100% RT score reflects a show that had transcended mere popularity into genuine critical affection.

bollymeter.basis: A 90% Rotten Tomatoes score placed Season 8 as the second-most reviewed season with some critics noting the end was in sight; the formula remained effective but the arc was contracting naturally.

seasons.review_body: Season 8 aired in late 2012 and drew some of the first critical commentary about the approaching end of Mark and Jeremy's shared story. The 90% RT score was a slight dip from the string of perfect scores, reflecting a small number of critics who sensed the show's best material had been spent. Fan and audience reception remained entirely loyal. The season continued refining the character arcs toward eventual resolution, with some episodes in this run representing the last truly explosive set pieces of the series' long run.
seasons.season_over_season: Slight critical contraction from the 100% run; still high-quality but for the first time the show's long character arc felt finite rather than inexhaustible.

bollymeter.basis: The 100% final-season RT score reflected a show that ended on its own terms rather than running dry; critics treated the finale as a proper valediction for one of British comedy's defining series.

seasons.review_body: The final season aired in November and December 2015, returning to a perfect 100% Rotten Tomatoes score. The finale lands with genuine affection, with Peep Show running for 12 years without losing either its formal ingenuity or its fundamental understanding of its characters. The closing episodes resolve Mark and Jeremy's long arcs in a way that stays tonally consistent with what came before: anticlimactic, uncomfortable, and funnier for it. Radio Times later named Peep Show the 13th greatest British sitcom of all time in a 2019 poll. The final season confirms the show as a completed work, not a cancelled one.
seasons.season_over_season: The series finale returns the show to a 100% RT score, a fitting send-off from critics who watched it sustain quality over 12 years; the ending is as uncomfortably perfect as the format always promised.

episode_reviews.title: Are We Going to Be Alright?
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series finale answers its own question with characteristic ambivalence. Mark and Jeremy end where they began - together by default, having failed at nearly everything else - and the show finds a note of melancholy resolution that is earned precisely because it refuses to be triumphant.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final image of Mark and Jeremy: together not because they chose it but because the universe offers them nothing better.
